in relation to which the sponsor has given the Commonwealth Secretary a notice in compliance with the exemption,

the vaping goods are not the subject of a determination by the Commonwealth Secretary, published on the Commonwealth Department’s website, that the supply of the goods be stopped or should be stopped because the Commonwealth Secretary is satisfied that the supply of the goods compromises public health and safety or the goods do not conform with a standard applicable to the goods, or
the vaping goods are covered by a section 41R determination.
This subsection applies in relation to the possession of the vaping goods by the person if—
the person—
is the holder of a licence or permission, granted under regulations made under the Customs Act 1901 of the Commonwealth, section 50, to import the vaping goods, or
is otherwise approved under those regulations to import the vaping goods, or
the person is the holder of a licence under the Commonwealth Therapeutic Goods Act, Part 3-3 that—
is in force, and
authorises a step in the manufacture of the vaping goods, or
the person is the holder of a conformity assessment document that applies to the vaping goods, or
both of the following apply—

the person is a wholesaler, pharmacist, medical practitioner or nurse practitioner who is the holder of a licence, or is otherwise authorised, under this Act to supply one or more substances included in the NSW Poisons Schedules, Schedule 3,
the possession of the vaping goods is in accordance with the licence or authority, or
both of the following apply—
the person has been given a section 41RC consent to possess the vaping goods,
the possession of the vaping goods is in accordance with the consent, or
if the vaping goods are covered by a section 41R determination—
the person is specified in the determination, or is included in a class of persons specified in the determination, in relation to the vaping goods, and
the possession of the vaping goods is in accordance with the determination.

heading.b: Prohibition on possession of vaping goods—less than commercial quantities

block.txt: A person is guilty of an offence if—
the person is a retailer in relation to retail premises in New South Wales, and
the person possesses a quantity of a kind of vaping goods at the retail premises, and
the quantity is less than the commercial quantity of the kind of vaping goods.
Maximum penalty—12 months imprisonment or 1,400 penalty units, or both.
A person is guilty of a strict liability offence if—
the person is a retailer in relation to retail premises in New South Wales, and
the person possesses a quantity of a kind of vaping goods at the retail premises, and
the quantity is less than the commercial quantity of the kind of vaping goods.
Maximum penalty—160 penalty units.
Subsections (1) and (2) do not apply if subsections (4) and (5) apply in relation to the possession of the vaping goods by the person.
This subsection applies in relation to the possession of the vaping goods by the person if—
the vaping goods are therapeutic goods included in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods, or
both of the following apply—
the vaping goods are therapeutic goods—

that are exempt goods under regulations made under the Commonwealth Therapeutic Goods Act, section 18(1) or an exempt device under regulations made under the Commonwealth Therapeutic Goods Act, section 41HA(1), and
in relation to which the sponsor has given the Commonwealth Secretary a notice in compliance with the exemption,

the vaping goods are not the subject of a determination by the Commonwealth Secretary, published on the Commonwealth Department’s website, that the supply of the goods be stopped or should be stopped because the Commonwealth Secretary is satisfied that the supply of the goods compromises public health and safety or the goods do not conform with a standard applicable to the goods, or
the vaping goods are covered by a section 41R determination.
This subsection applies in relation to the possession of the vaping goods by the person if—
both of the following apply—

the person is a wholesaler, pharmacist, medical practitioner or nurse practitioner who is the holder of a licence, or is otherwise authorised, under this Act to supply one or more substances included in the NSW Poisons Schedules, Schedule 3,
the possession of the vaping goods is in accordance with the licence or authority, or
both of the following apply—
the person has been given a section 41RC consent to possess the vaping goods,
the possession of the vaping goods is in accordance with the consent, or
if the vaping goods are covered by a section 41R determination—
the person is specified in the determination, or is included in a class of persons specified in the determination, in relation to the vaping goods, and
the possession of the vaping goods is in accordance with the determination.
Subsections (1) and (2) do not apply in relation to the possession of the vaping goods by the person if—
the vaping goods are for use by the person personally, and
the quantity of the vaping goods is not more than the permitted quantity of the kind of vaping goods.
In this section—
permitted quantity, of a kind of vaping goods, has the same meaning as in the Commonwealth Therapeutic Goods Act, section 41QD(10).
retail premises means either of the following types of premises, whether or not the premises are used wholly or predominantly for the relevant purpose—
premises from which goods or services are available for supply, or are supplied, to a consumer, or
premises that are used in connection with the supply of goods or services to a consumer.
retailer, in relation to retail premises in New South Wales, means any of the following—
an owner, lessee or occupier of the retail premises,
a person conducting a business or undertaking at, or in connection or association with, the retail premises,
a director, officer or agent of a person referred to in paragraph (a) or (b),
a person performing work in any capacity, including an employee or a contractor, for, or on behalf of, a person referred to in paragraph (a), (b) or (c) at or in connection with the retail premises.

heading.b: Application of Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws
Application of Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws

block.txt: The Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws, as in force from time to time and as modified by the regulations, apply as a law of New South Wales and are referred to in this Act as the applied provisions.
The Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws apply as a law of New South Wales as if the laws extended to things done or omitted to be done—
by a person who is not a corporation, and
during trade or commerce within the limits of New South Wales.
The regulations under this Act may modify the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws for the purposes of this section.
The Acts Interpretation Act 1901 and the Legislation Act 2003 of the Commonwealth, as in force from time to time, apply—
as laws of New South Wales in relation to the interpretation of the applied provisions, and
as if the applied provisions were an Act of the Commonwealth or regulations or orders under an Act of the Commonwealth, as the case requires.
The Interpretation Act 1987 does not apply to the applied provisions.

heading.b: Functions of Commonwealth Minister, Commonwealth Secretary and others

block.txt: The Commonwealth Minister has the same functions under the applied provisions as the Commonwealth Minister has under the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws as the laws apply to the Commonwealth.
The Commonwealth Secretary has the same functions under the applied provisions as the Commonwealth Secretary has under the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws as the laws apply to the Commonwealth.

Without limiting subsection (2), the Commonwealth Secretary has the function of including goods in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods kept under the applied provisions and is authorised to cancel the inclusion of goods in the Register in accordance with the applied provisions.

An authorised person, authorised officer or official analyst appointed under the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws has the same functions under the applied provisions as the person, officer or analyst has under the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws as the laws apply to the Commonwealth.

A delegation by the Commonwealth Minister or the Commonwealth Secretary under the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws is taken to extend to, and have effect for the purposes of, the corresponding provision of the applied provisions.
The appointment of a person to an office or position under a provision of the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws is taken to extend to, and have effect for the purposes of, the applied provisions.
In this section—
Commonwealth Minister means the Minister responsible for administering the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws.

The Commonwealth administrative laws apply as a law of New South Wales to matters arising in relation to the applied provisions as if the applied provisions were laws of the Commonwealth and not a law of New South Wales.
For the purposes of the law of New South Wales, a matter arising in relation to the applied provisions—
is taken to be a matter arising in relation to the laws of the Commonwealth in the same way as if the applied provisions were laws of the Commonwealth, and
is taken not to be a matter arising in relation to the law of New South Wales.
Subsection (2) has effect for the purposes of the law of New South Wales except as provided for by the regulations.
A provision of a Commonwealth administrative law applying because of this section purporting to confer jurisdiction on a federal court is taken not to have the effect.

If a Commonwealth administrative law, which applies because of this section, confers a function on a Commonwealth officer or authority, the law also confers the same function on the officer or authority in relation to a matter arising in relation to the applied provisions.

In exercising a function conferred by this section, the Commonwealth officer or authority must act as nearly as is practicable as the officer or authority would act in exercising the same function under the Commonwealth administrative law.
A function conferred on a Commonwealth officer or authority because of this section must not be exercised by an officer or authority of New South Wales.
In this section—
Commonwealth administrative laws means the following Acts of the Commonwealth and the regulations under the Acts—
the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024,
the Freedom of Information Act 1982,
the Ombudsman Act 1976,
the Privacy Act 1988.
An offence against the applied provisions must be treated as if it were an offence against a law of the Commonwealth.
The purposes for which an offence against the applied provisions must be treated as an offence against a law of the Commonwealth include, without limitation, the following—
the investigation and prosecution of offences,
the arrest, custody, bail, trial and conviction of offenders or persons charged with offences,
proceedings relating to a matter referred to in paragraph (a) or (b),
appeals and reviews relating to criminal proceedings and to proceedings relating to a matter referred to in paragraph (a) or (b),
the sentencing, punishment and release of persons convicted of offences,
fines, penalties and forfeitures,
liability to make reparation in connection with offences,
proceeds of crime,
spent convictions.

The Commonwealth laws relating to the matters specified in subsection (2) apply as a law of New South Wales in relation to an offence against the applied provisions as if the applied provisions were laws of the Commonwealth and not a law of New South Wales.
For the purposes of the law of New South Wales, an offence against the applied provisions—
is taken to be an offence against the laws of the Commonwealth, as if the applied provisions were laws of the Commonwealth, and
is taken not to be an offence against the law of New South Wales.
Subsection (4) has effect for the purposes of the law of New South Wales except as provided by the regulations.

heading.b: Functions of Commonwealth officers and authorities relating to offences

block.txt: If a Commonwealth law, which applies because of section 89, confers a function in relation to an offence against the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws on a Commonwealth officer or authority, the law also confers the same function on the officer or authority in relation to an offence against the corresponding provision of the applied provisions.

In exercising a function conferred by this section, the Commonwealth officer or authority must act as nearly as practicable as the officer or authority would act in exercising the same function in relation to an offence against the corresponding provision of the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws.

heading.b: No double jeopardy for offences against applied provisions

block.txt: An offender is not liable to be punished for an offence against the applied provisions for an act or omission if—
the act or omission is an offence against both the applied provisions and the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws, and
the offender has been punished for the offence under the Commonwealth therapeutic goods laws.

heading.b: Commonwealth may keep fees paid to Commonwealth Secretary

block.txt: The Commonwealth may keep fees paid to, or recovered by, the Commonwealth Secretary for the exercise of functions conferred on the Commonwealth Secretary by the applied provisions.
A reference in this Part to an authorised officer does not include a police officer.

heading.b: Powers to require information and records

block.txt: An authorised officer may, by written notice given to a person, require the person to provide the authorised officer with information or records, or both, that the authorised officer requires for ensuring compliance with this Act and the regulations, including compliance with the conditions of a licence, approval or DMT authority (referred to in this Chapter as compliance purposes).
A notice must specify—
the way in which the information or records must be provided, and
a reasonable time by which the information or records must be provided.
A notice may only require a person to provide existing records that are—
in the person’s possession, or
within the person’s power to obtain lawfully.
The authorised officer to whom records are provided under this section may make copies of the records.
Records must be provided in written form, unless the notice otherwise provides.

An authorised officer may require a person to answer questions in relation to a relevant matter if the authorised officer suspects on reasonable grounds that the person has knowledge of the relevant matter.

An authorised officer may, by written notice given to a corporation, require the corporation to nominate, within the time specified in the notice, one or more of the following, who has relevant knowledge about the corporation’s activities, as the corporation’s representative for the purposes of answering questions under this section—
a director of the corporation,
an officer of the corporation,
a contractor.
Answers given by a person nominated by the corporation bind the corporation.

An authorised officer may, by written notice, require a person to attend at a specified place and time to answer questions if attendance at the place is reasonably required for the questions to be properly put and answered.
The place and time at which a person may be required to attend under subsection (4) must be a place and time nominated by the authorised officer that is reasonable in the circumstances.
In this section—
relevant matter means a matter in relation to which information is reasonably required for compliance purposes.

An authorised officer may arrange for questions and answers to questions given under this Part to be recorded if the authorised officer has informed the person who will be questioned that a record will be made.
A record may be made using—
audio or audio visual equipment, or
another method determined by the authorised officer.
A copy of the record must be provided by the authorised officer to the person who is questioned as soon as practicable after the copy is made.
A record may be made under this section despite the provisions of another law.

heading.b: Power to require name and address

block.txt: An authorised officer may require a person who the authorised officer suspects on reasonable grounds to have committed, or to be committing, an offence against this Act or the regulations to state the person’s full name, date of birth and residential address.
A requirement made under this Part does not affect the privilege against self-incrimination as it applies to an individual.
An authorised officer may enter premises at a reasonable time for compliance purposes.
Entry to premises may be effected under this Act—
with the use of reasonable force, and
with or without the authority of a search warrant.
This Part does not empower an authorised officer to enter a part of premises used only for residential purposes without—
the permission of the occupier, or
the authority of a search warrant.
An authorised officer may apply to an issuing officer for the issue of a search warrant for premises if the authorised officer believes on reasonable grounds—
a requirement imposed by or under this Act is being or has been contravened at the premises, or
there is, in or on the premises, a matter or thing connected with an offence under this Act or the regulations.
An issuing officer to whom an application is made may, if satisfied there are reasonable grounds for doing so, issue a search warrant authorising an authorised officer named in the warrant—
to enter the premises, and
to exercise a function of an authorised officer under this Chapter.
The Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002, Part 5, Division 4 applies to a search warrant issued under this section.
In this section—
issuing officer means an authorised officer within the meaning of the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002.

heading.b: Powers permitted to be exercised on premises

block.txt: An authorised officer may, at premises lawfully entered, do anything the authorised officer considers necessary to be done for compliance purposes, including the following—
search the premises,
examine and inspect a thing, including open and examine a receptacle, container or package,
take and remove samples of a thing, including for analysis,
make examinations, inquiries or tests the authorised officer considers necessary,
take photographs or other recordings the authorised officer considers necessary,
require records or other documents to be produced for inspection,
examine, inspect and remove records or other documents,
copy records or other documents,
seize a thing if the authorised officer has reasonable grounds for believing—
the thing is connected with an offence against this Act or the regulations, or
the owner of the thing cannot readily be identified or determined,
move a seized thing from the place where the thing is seized or leave the thing at the place where the thing is seized and take reasonable action to restrict access to the thing,
direct the occupier of the premises where a thing is seized to keep the thing at the premises or at another place under the control of the occupier,
require a person holding or required to hold a wholesaler licence, obtain licence, approval, OTP registration or DMT authority to produce it for inspection,
anything else authorised by or under this Act.

The power to examine and inspect a thing includes a power to use reasonable force to break open or otherwise access a container or other thing being used, or suspected of being used, to hold or contain another thing.
The power to seize a thing connected with an offence includes a power to seize—
a thing for or with which the offence has been committed, and
a thing providing evidence of the commission of the offence, and
a thing used for the purposes of committing the offence.
The power to do a thing under this section—
includes a power to require or arrange for the thing to be done, and
may be exercised without the consent of the owner of the thing.
In this section, a reference to an offence includes a reference to an offence there are reasonable grounds for believing has been committed.

heading.b: Power to require name and address

block.txt: An authorised officer may, at premises lawfully entered, require a person who the authorised officer suspects on reasonable grounds to have committed, or to be committing, an offence against this Act or the regulations to state the person’s full name, date of birth and residential address.

An authorised officer may require the owner or occupier of premises, or another person in or on premises, other than a public place, to provide the reasonable assistance the authorised officer specifies for the purposes of exercising the authorised officer’s functions under this Part in relation to the premises.
The requirement may be given—
as a verbal direction to the person, or
by written notice to the person.

In exercising a power of entering or searching premises under this Part, or doing anything else on premises under this Act, an authorised officer must use no more force that is reasonably necessary to exercise the power.
In this Part—
seized thing means a thing seized by an authorised officer under Part 5.2.

A seized thing must be released at the end of the period of 6 months after the seizure (the return period) unless, before the end of the return period, the thing is forfeited to the State under this Part.
The Health Secretary may, by written notice given to the apparent owner, extend the return period for a particular seized thing.
A seized thing may be released—
by or at the direction of—
the authorised officer who seized the thing, or
the Health Secretary, and
to the owner of the thing or the person who had possession, care, custody or control of the thing at the time the thing was seized.
This section does not—
require the release of a seized thing that was damaged or destroyed during analysis, or
prevent a seized thing from being released before the end of the return period.

heading.b: Forfeiture of seized things by order

block.txt: A seized thing is forfeited to the State if the Health Secretary makes an order under this section declaring the forfeiture of the thing.
The Health Secretary may, by written order, declare a seized thing to be forfeited to the State if satisfied that—
a person has been convicted of an offence in connection with the seized thing, or
the owner of the seized thing cannot be found despite inquiries being made that are reasonable in the circumstances, or
the seized thing cannot be returned to the owner for other reasons despite efforts being made that are reasonable in the circumstances, or
the return of the seized thing would pose an unacceptable risk to the health or safety of a human or animal, whether or not identifiable, or
other prescribed grounds.
At least 21 days before making an order, the Health Secretary must give written notice to the apparent owner of a seized thing of the intention to declare the seized thing to be forfeited.
The notice must specify a period within which the apparent owner may make submissions to the Health Secretary before the order is made.
The Health Secretary must consider any submissions made within the specified period.
The Health Secretary is not required to give notice to the apparent owner of a seized thing if—
an authorised officer has given a written certificate that the authorised officer is unable to return the seized thing to the owner, or
the Health Secretary is satisfied that—
the owner of the seized thing cannot be found despite inquiries being made that are reasonable in the circumstances, or
the seized thing cannot be returned to the owner for other reasons despite efforts being made that are reasonable in the circumstances.

heading.b: Forfeiture of seized things with consent

block.txt: The owner of a seized thing, or the person who had possession, care, custody or control of the thing at the time the thing was seized, may give written consent for the forfeiture of the thing.
The seized thing is forfeited to the State when the written consent is given.

heading.b: Order for expenses to be paid

block.txt: If a person from whom a seized thing has been seized is convicted of an offence in connection with the seized thing, the Supreme Court or Local Court may order the person to pay the Health Secretary an amount the Court considers appropriate to cover the reasonable costs of—
seizing the thing, and
dealing with the thing under this Part, and
conducting an analysis for which the thing is submitted.
Before making an order, the Court may require specified notice to be given to specified persons, as the Court considers appropriate.

heading.b: Storage of and interference with seized things

block.txt: Subject to the directions of the Health Secretary, a seized thing may be kept or stored at—
the premises at which the thing was seized, or
another place the authorised officer who seized the thing considers appropriate.
A person must not remove, alter or interfere with a seized thing without the approval of an authorised officer or the Health Secretary.
Maximum penalty for subsection (2)—Tier 5 penalty.
A seized thing forfeited under this Part may be disposed of in a way directed by the Health Secretary, whether generally or in a particular circumstance or class of circumstances.

heading.b: Offence—contravention of requirement made by authorised officer

block.txt: A person must not, without reasonable excuse, contravene a requirement made of the person by an authorised officer exercising a power under this Chapter.
Maximum penalty—Tier 4 penalty.

A person is not guilty of an offence of failing to comply with a requirement to provide records or information or to answer a question unless the person was warned on the occasion that failure to comply is an offence.
The Health Secretary and an authorised officer may vary or revoke a notice given under this Chapter by a subsequent notice or notices.
Without limiting subsection (1), a notice may be varied by extending the time for complying with the notice.

heading.b: Destruction of things surrendered by enforcement agencies

block.txt: This section applies if a relevant enforcement agency—
lawfully seizes a thing, and
is not required under law to return the thing to the person from whom it was seized or to the owner.
An authorised recipient may—
agree to receive a thing that the relevant enforcement agency lawfully surrenders to the authorised recipient, and
destroy, or authorise the destruction of, the thing if—
a decision is made not to prosecute a person for an offence under this Act or another Act in connection with the thing, or
a decision is not made within 6 months of the surrender of the thing to prosecute a person for an offence under this Act or another Act in connection with the thing.
Damages or other compensation is not payable to a person for the destruction of a thing in accordance with this section.
In this section—
authorised recipient means the Health Secretary or a person authorised by the Health Secretary for the purposes of this section.
relevant enforcement agency means—
the Australian Border Force, or
another prescribed entity of an Australian jurisdiction with power to seize things that are or may be therapeutic goods.
The Health Secretary may give a person a written notice (a compliance notice) if the Health Secretary believes the person—
is contravening—
a provision of this Act or the regulations, or
a condition of a wholesaler licence, obtain licence, approval, OTP registration or DMT authority, or
has contravened a provision or condition in circumstances making it likely the contravention will continue or be repeated.
A compliance notice may require the person—
to remedy the contravention, or
to prevent a likely contravention from occurring, or
to remedy the things or operations causing the contravention or likely contravention.
A compliance notice must specify—
the grounds on which the compliance notice is given, including the particular contravention on which the compliance notice is based, and
the compliance period.
A compliance notice may include directions about the measures to be taken to remedy the contravention or prevent the likely contravention.
Before the end of the compliance period, the Health Secretary may, by written notice to the person, extend the compliance period for a compliance notice.
A person must comply with the compliance notice within the compliance period.
Maximum penalty—Tier 4 penalty.
The Health Secretary may vary or revoke a compliance notice.
A compliance notice is not invalid only because of—
a formal defect or irregularity in the compliance notice, unless the defect or irregularity causes or is likely to cause substantial injustice, or
a failure to use the correct name of the person to whom the compliance notice is issued if the compliance notice—
sufficiently identifies the person, and
is given to the person in accordance with this Act.
In this section—
compliance period, for a compliance notice, means the period within which a person is required to comply with the compliance notice and includes the period as extended under subsection (5).
A person to whom a compliance notice is issued under section 115 may apply to the Health Secretary for a review of the decision to issue the compliance notice.
An application must be—
in an approved form, and
made within the compliance period for the compliance notice under section 115.
The Health Secretary may refuse to consider an application for review if the Health Secretary—
has considered an application for review in relation to the same compliance notice within the previous 6 months, and
is not satisfied there has been a material change in relevant circumstances.
The Health Secretary must determine an application for review by—
confirming the compliance notice, or
varying the compliance notice, or
revoking the compliance notice.

block.txt: If a corporation contravenes a provision of this Act or the regulations, each person who is a director of the corporation or who is concerned in the management of the corporation is taken to have contravened the same provision if the person knowingly authorised or permitted the contravention.
A person may be proceeded against and convicted under a provision as provided by subsection (1) whether or not the corporation has been proceeded against or convicted under the provision.
This section does not affect the liability imposed on a corporation for an offence committed by the corporation under this Act or the regulations.
This section applies to a provision of this Act or the regulations requiring a person to do, or stop doing, something (a continuing requirement provision) regardless of whether—
the requirement is imposed by a notice or in another way, or
the person is required to do, or stop doing, something within a specified period.
A person who is guilty of an offence because the person contravenes a continuing requirement provision—
continues, until the requirement is complied with and despite the fact a specified period has expired or time has passed, to be liable to comply with the requirement, and
is guilty of a continuing offence for each day the contravention continues.
This section does not apply to an offence if the relevant provision of this Act or the regulations does not provide for a penalty for a continuing offence.
A provision that has a Tier 1–5 penalty includes a penalty for a continuing offence.
This section does not apply to the extent that a requirement imposed on a person is revoked.
Proceedings for an offence under this Act or the regulations may be dealt with—
summarily before the Local Court, or
summarily before the Supreme Court in its summary jurisdiction.
Subsection (1) does not apply in relation to proceedings for an offence against section 85B(1), 85C(3) or 85C(5).
Proceedings for an offence must be commenced not later than 2 years from when the offence was alleged to have been committed.
An authorised officer may issue a penalty notice to a person if it appears to the officer the person has committed a penalty notice offence.
A penalty notice offence is an offence against this Act or the regulations prescribed by the regulations as a penalty notice offence.
The Fines Act 1996 applies to a penalty notice issued under this section.

The Fines Act 1996 provides that, if a person issued with a penalty notice does not wish to have the matter determined by a court, the person may pay the amount specified in the notice and is not liable to further proceedings for the alleged offence.

The amount payable under a penalty notice issued under this section is the amount prescribed for the alleged offence by the regulations, not exceeding the maximum amount of penalty that could be imposed for the offence by a court.
This section does not limit the operation of another provision of, or made under, this Act or another Act relating to proceedings that may be taken for offences.
A relevant person does not commit an offence against this Act or the regulations for an activity carried out in the exercise of functions under this Act or the regulations.
A relevant person, or an individual acting under the direction of a relevant person, is not personally subject to civil liability for anything done or omitted to be done—
in good faith, and
for the purposes of exercising functions under this Act or the regulations.
In this section—
civil liability includes an action, claim or demand.
relevant person means the following—
the Health Secretary or a delegate of the Health Secretary,
an authorised officer,
a member of the Clinical Advisory Committee,
a member of the Regulatory Advisory Committee.

heading.b: Exclusion of civil liability of State and State authorities

block.txt: This section applies to civil proceedings for compensation brought against the State or an authority of the State.

Compensation is not payable in civil proceedings to the extent the claim is based on alleged negligence, defamation or other breach of duty, including statutory duty, arising because of the exercise of, or the failure to exercise, functions under this Act or the regulations in good faith.
In this section—
compensation includes damages and other forms of monetary compensation.

A certificate purportedly issued by the Health Secretary or an authorised Health certifier stating a matter specified in subsection (2) was, or was not the case, at a specified time or during a specified period is—
admissible in legal proceedings under this Act or another Act, and
prima facie evidence of the matters stated.
The following matters may be certified in a certificate issued under this section—
a person had, or did not have, a particular authorisation,
an authorisation was, or was not, subject to a particular condition, restriction, limitation or other requirement,
a person was, or was not, an authorised officer or analyst,
other prescribed matters relating to the enforcement or administration of this Act or the regulations.
In this section—
authorisation includes an approval, exemption or other authority issued by the Health Secretary under this Act or the regulations.

authorised Health certifier means an employee of the Ministry of Health with written authorisation, whether generally or specifically, from the Health Secretary to issue a certificate under this section.
An analyst may give a certificate of the results of an analysis of a substance provided for analysis under this Act if the analyst—
analysed the substance, or
supervised or directed the analysis of the substance.
A certificate purportedly issued by an analyst under this section about the results of an analysis is—
admissible in legal proceedings under this Act or another Act, and
prima facie evidence of the matters stated.
A certificate purportedly issued by an interstate analyst under corresponding Australian legislation about the results of the analysis of a substance is—
admissible in legal proceedings under this Act or another Act, and
prima facie evidence of the matters stated.
An analysis to which a certificate referred to in subsection (3) relates is taken to be an analysis of a substance provided under this Act.
In this section—
interstate analyst means a person, however described, who analysed, or who supervised or directed the analysis of, a substance for the purposes of corresponding Australian legislation.
This section applies to proceedings for a contravention of a provision of this Act or the regulations.

Evidence that a substance or good is, for the purposes of supply or dispensing, represented as being or including a particular therapeutic good is prima facie evidence that the substance or good is or includes the particular therapeutic good.
A substance or good is represented as being or including a particular therapeutic good for subsection (2) if —
a name or description commonly used for the therapeutic good is also used for the substance or good, or

the substance or good, or the container, is marked or labelled in the way that the therapeutic good or a thing including a therapeutic good, or the container, are required by the regulations to be marked or labelled, or
the substance or good, or the container, is marked or labelled in another way to indicate it is, includes or may include the therapeutic good.
In this section—

label includes to attach a tag, brand, mark or written statement to, or use a tag, brand, mark or written statement in connection with, a substance or good or a container or package containing the substance or good.

heading.b: Regulatory Advisory Committee and Clinical Advisory Committee

block.txt: The Regulatory Advisory Committee is established by this Act.
The function of the Committee is to advise the Health Secretary on matters referred to it by the Health Secretary relating to the following—
the operation, administration or amendment of this Act, the regulations and the NSW Poisons Schedules, including proposals to make, alter or repeal the regulations,
therapeutic goods or stock medicines,
the scheduling of substances under the Commonwealth Therapeutic Goods Act.
The Committee also has other functions conferred or imposed on it by or under this Act or another Act.
The Committee must consist of not less than 9, and not more than 15, members appointed by the Health Secretary.
The Health Secretary must appoint the following—
a person nominated by the Commissioner of Police,
a person nominated by SafeWork NSW,
a person nominated by the Australian Medical Association,
a person nominated by the New South Wales branch of the Pharmacy Guild of Australia,
a person nominated by the New South Wales branch of the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia.
The Health Secretary may appoint persons who the Health Secretary considers have qualifications or experience in the following areas—
medical, dental, nursing and midwifery,
veterinary practice,
industrial use of scheduled substances, including in primary industry,
pharmacology,
toxicology,
the medicines manufacturing and distribution industries,
the development of medicines and the regulation of scheduled substances, including their registration as therapeutic goods under the Commonwealth Therapeutic Goods Act,
assessing the risk of harm to humans, animals or the environment arising in connection with therapeutic goods,
as a consumer of therapeutic goods.
The Health Secretary may also appoint persons who the Health Secretary considers have prescribed qualifications or experience.
The Health Secretary must appoint a member of the Committee as Chairperson.
Schedule 1 contains provisions relating to the members and procedure of the Committee.
The Clinical Advisory Committee is established by this Act.
The Committee has the following functions—
to make recommendations to the Health Secretary about applications for approvals and existing approvals,
to advise the Health Secretary on other matters referred to the Committee by the Health Secretary,
prescribed functions.
The Committee must consist of at least 6 members appointed by the Health Secretary.
Each member must be a medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or other prescribed health practitioner.
The Health Secretary must appoint a member of the Committee as Chairperson.
Schedule 1 contains provisions relating to the members and procedure of the Committee.

heading.b: Information required from Health Care Complaints Commission and certain health practitioner bodies

block.txt: For the purposes of exercising its function under section 128(2)(a), the Clinical Advisory Committee may, by written notice to a relevant body, require a relevant body to provide information that the Committee reasonably requires to exercise the function.
A relevant body must comply with a requirement given under this section.
This section applies despite any provision of the Health Care Complaints Act 1993 or the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law (NSW).
In this section—
relevant body means the following—
Health Care Complaints Commission,
Medical Council of New South Wales,
Medical Board of Australia,
Nursing and Midwifery Council of New South Wales,
Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia.
The Regulatory Advisory Committee and the Clinical Advisory Committee may—
establish subcommittees for the purposes of assisting the Committee in the exercise of the Committee’s functions under this Act, and
appoint as a member of a subcommittee a person the Committee considers to be qualified to be a member of the subcommittee.
The members of a subcommittee do not need to be members of the Committee.

The Health Secretary may, by written instrument, appoint each of the following to be an authorised officer, either generally or in relation to a particular function exercisable by authorised officers under this Act or the regulations—
an employee of the Ministry of Health,
a member of the NSW Health Service,
other prescribed persons or classes of persons.
An appointment may apply to a specified person or to persons of a specified class.
An appointment may be unconditional, or subject to conditions or limitations.
An appointment has effect for the period specified in the instrument of appointment or, if no period is specified, until revoked by the Health Secretary.
The Heath Secretary may, by written instrument, revoke or amend an appointment under this section.
If an appointment of an authorised officer is made by reference to a particular office, the person appointed ceases to be an authorised officer if the person ceases to hold the office.

heading.b: Police officers taken to be authorised officers

block.txt: A police officer is taken to be an authorised officer for this Act, other than for the purposes of Part 5.1.

This Act does not limit the functions of a police officer under the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 or another law, including the functions of a police officer in relation to seized items.
Subject to the terms of an authorised officer’s appointment, an authorised officer has the functions conferred or imposed on an authorised officer by or under this Act or another Act.

heading.b: Certificate of authority for authorised officers

block.txt: The Health Secretary must ensure an authorised officer is issued with a certificate of authority.
The certificate of authority must—
specify it is issued under this Act, and
give the name of the person to whom it is issued, and
include a recent photograph of the person to whom it is issued, and
describe the nature of the powers conferred and the source of the powers, and
specify the date, if any, on which it expires, and
describe the kind of premises to which the power extends, and
be signed by the person issuing the certificate and specify the capacity in which the person is acting in issuing the certificate.
A certificate of authority may be issued in the form of a card.

A person who has ceased to be an authorised officer must not, without reasonable excuse, fail to return to the Health Secretary, within the period specified by the Health Secretary in a request for the return of the certificate, a certificate of authority issued to the person by the Health Secretary.
Maximum penalty—Tier 5 penalty.
An authorised officer must not exercise a function conferred by or under this Act unless a certificate of authority has been issued to the authorised officer.

When exercising the functions of an authorised officer under this Act, the officer must, if requested to do so by a person affected by the exercise of the function, produce to the person the officer’s certificate of authority.
This section does not apply to—
a power conferred by a search warrant, or
an authorised officer who is a police officer.
An authorised officer exercising a function conferred by or under this Act may exercise the function with the assistance of another person that the authorised officer considers necessary.
The person may accompany an authorised officer and take all reasonable steps to assist the authorised officer in the exercise of the authorised officer’s functions under this Act.
A person must not resist or obstruct an authorised officer in the exercise of the officer’s functions under this Act.
Maximum penalty—Tier 3 penalty.
A person must not assault, abuse or threaten an authorised officer or encourage another person to do so.
Maximum penalty—Tier 3 penalty.
A person must not impersonate an authorised officer.
Maximum penalty—Tier 3 penalty.
The Health Secretary may, by written instrument, appoint a person as an analyst for the purposes of this Act.
An analyst appointed for the purposes of this Act is also an analyst under the Drug Misuse and Trafficking Act 1985.
An appointment may apply to a specified person or to persons of a specified class.
An appointment may be unconditional, or subject to conditions or limitations.
An appointment has effect for the period specified in the instrument of appointment or, if no period is specified, until revoked by the Health Secretary.
The Health Secretary may, by written instrument, revoke or amend an appointment under this section.
If an appointment of an analyst is made by reference to a particular office, the person appointed ceases to be an analyst if the person ceases to hold the office.
A person may submit for analysis under this section a substance or goods seized under this Act.
An analyst must carry out or personally supervise the carrying out of an analysis of a substance or goods submitted to the analyst for analysis.

An analyst who has carried out or personally supervised the carrying out of an analysis of the substance or goods may, and must on request, issue a certificate of analysis setting out the results of the analysis.

The owner of the substance or goods, or the person in whose possession or under whose control the substance or goods were when they were seized, is entitled to be given a copy of the certificate of analysis relating to the substance or goods on payment of the prescribed fee, if any.

heading.b: Offence—use of analysis for trade purposes or advertisement

block.txt: A person must not, for trade purposes or advertisement, use—
the results of an analysis carried out for the purposes of this Act, or
a certificate of analysis issued under section 138(3).
Maximum penalty—Tier 5 penalty.

heading.b: Health Secretary may make public health risk authorisation orders

block.txt: The Health Secretary may make an order (a public health risk authorisation order) that authorises a specified person or class of persons to possess, supply, wholesale supply, obtain wholesale supply, administer, dispense, use, prescribe, manufacture, store or dispose of therapeutic goods or stock medicines.
The Health Secretary may make a public health risk authorisation order if the Health Secretary considers on reasonable grounds that—
a situation presents, or is likely to present, a risk to the health or safety of humans or animals, and
the order is necessary or convenient to deal with the risk and the possible consequences.
A public health risk authorisation order must specify the following—
the purpose of the order, including the risk being dealt with,
the person or class of persons authorised by the order,
the activity the person or class of persons specified in the order is authorised to do,
the therapeutic goods or stock medicines in relation to which the person or class of persons is authorised to undertake the activity,
other conditions to which the authorisation is subject.
A public health risk authorisation order is not invalid just because the matter referred to in subsection (3)(a) is not specified in the order.
A public health risk authorisation order must be published in the Gazette as soon as practicable after it is made.

The Health Secretary must consult with the Secretary of the Department of Regional NSW before making a public health risk authorisation order that relates to, or affects, the health or safety of animals.
Failure to comply with subsection (5) or (6) does not invalidate the public health risk authorisation order.
The operation of a public health risk authorisation order may be extended by the making of a further order under this section on or before the expiry of the order.
The regulations may prescribe other requirements to be complied with before a public health risk authorisation order may be made or extended.

heading.b: Duration of public health risk authorisation orders

block.txt: A public health risk authorisation order commences on—
the day specified in the order, or
if no day is specified—the day on which the order is published in the Gazette.
A public health risk authorisation order may commence on a day before the day it is published in the Gazette.
Unless earlier revoked, a public health risk authorisation order expires at the end of—
90 days after it commences, or
an earlier day specified in the order.

heading.b: Effect of public health risk authorisation orders

block.txt: A person is not prevented from taking action authorised by a public health risk authorisation order by anything in this Act, the Drug Misuse and Trafficking Act 1985 or the Stock Medicines Act 1989.
To avoid doubt, a public health risk authorisation order authorises action, but it does not impose an obligation on a person.

heading.b: Health Secretary may make supply prohibition orders

block.txt: The Health Secretary may make an order (a supply prohibition order) that prohibits the supply of a substance specified in the order if satisfied that the substance should not be supplied pending the evaluation of the toxic or deleterious properties of the substance.
A supply prohibition order must be published in the Gazette as soon as practicable after it is made.
Failure to comply with subsection (2) does not invalidate the supply prohibition order.
A supply prohibition order commences on—
the day specified in the order, or
if no day is specified—the day on which the order is published in the Gazette.
Unless earlier revoked, a supply prohibition order expires at the end of—
90 days after it commences, or
an earlier day specified in the order.
A person must not contravene a supply prohibition order.
Maximum penalty for subsection (6)—Tier 4 penalty.

heading.b: Health Secretary may recover fees and charges

block.txt: A fee or other charge payable under this Act, the regulations or the applied provisions may be recovered by the Health Secretary as a debt due to the Crown in a court of competent jurisdiction.
The Health Secretary may refund, waive or postpone the whole or part of a fee or other charge payable under this Act, the regulations or the applied provisions.
A document authorised or required by this Act or the regulations to be given to a person may be given by the following methods—
for an individual—by personal delivery to the person,
by post to the address specified by the person for the giving of documents of the kind,
for an individual who does not have a specified address—by post to the residential or business address of the person last known to the person giving the document,
for a corporation—by post to the registered office or other office of the corporation or by leaving it at the office with a person who is apparently more than 16 years of age,
by email to an email address specified by the person for the giving of documents of the kind,
by another method authorised by the regulations for the giving of documents of the kind.
This section does not affect the operation of provisions of a law or of the rules of a court authorising a document to be given to or served on a person by another method.
A person must not disclose information obtained in connection with the administration or execution of this Act unless the disclosure is made—
with the consent of the person from whom the information was obtained, or
in connection with the administration or execution of this Act or the regulations, or
for the purposes of legal proceedings arising out of this Act or the regulations, or
in prescribed circumstances, or
with other lawful excuse.
Maximum penalty—Tier 2 penalty.
This Act binds the Crown in right of New South Wales and, to the extent the legislative power of the Parliament of New South Wales permits, the Crown in all its other capacities.
The Minister must review this Act to determine whether—
the policy objectives of the Act remain valid, and
the terms of the Act remain appropriate for securing the objectives.
The review must be undertaken as soon as possible after the period of 5 years from the commencement of this section.
A report on the outcome of the review must be tabled in each House of Parliament within 12 months after the end of the period of 5 years.
The Governor may make regulations, not inconsistent with this Act, about—
matters required or permitted to be prescribed by this Act, or
matters necessary or convenient to be prescribed for carrying out or giving effect to this Act.
Without limiting the Interpretation Act 1987, section 42, the regulations may—
apply to—
specified therapeutic goods or classes of therapeutic goods, or
specified persons or classes of persons, or
specified circumstances, and
if made for the purposes of including or excluding a thing from a definition— apply generally or be limited to—
specified provisions of this Act, or
specified activities, or
therapeutic goods for specified provisions of this Act.
If the regulations may provide for the Health Secretary to determine a matter, the regulations may provide for the Health Secretary to determine the matter as follows—
generally or limited to a particular person, premises or circumstances or class of persons, premises or circumstances,
generally or limited to a particular scheduled substance or other therapeutic goods or class of scheduled substance or other therapeutic goods,
unconditionally or subject to conditions.
The regulations may apply, adopt or incorporate, wholly or in part and with or without modification, an Appendix of the Commonwealth Poisons Standard.

The regulations may apply, adopt or incorporate, wholly or in part and with or without modification, a standard, rule, code, specification, method or publication, as in force at a particular time or as in force from time to time, prescribed or published by an authority or body, whether or not it is a New South Wales authority or body.
The regulations may create offences, including continuing offences, punishable by a penalty not exceeding—
for a corporation—100 penalty units, or
for an individual—20 penalty units.
Without limiting section 149, the regulations may provide for the following—
the calculation for the purposes of the NSW Poisons Schedules of percentages for liquid preparations,
preparing, supplying, storing, labelling, packaging, handling, carrying and delivering scheduled substances and therapeutic goods,
the administration, possession and use of scheduled substances and therapeutic goods,
wholesaler and obtain licences, approvals, OTP registrations and DMT authorities,
sampling, examining, testing and analysing therapeutic goods,

the quantities of Schedule 4D substances, or the determination of the quantities of Schedule 4D substances, for the purposes of a possession for deemed supply offence under the Drug Misuse and Trafficking Act 1985,
conditions to be complied with when preparing, supplying, storing, packing, handling, carrying and delivering scheduled substances and other prescribed therapeutic goods,
records required to be kept for the purposes of activities relating to scheduled substances or other prescribed therapeutic goods,
the persons authorised to order or receive scheduled substances or other prescribed therapeutic goods on behalf of another person or body,
employees at a residential aged care facility or a correctional centre
the use of medical devices, including restrictions, conditions and offences,
the loss, theft, altering or tampering of prescriptions,
review of decisions made by the Health Secretary or other persons under this Act or the regulations, including the way in which reviews are to be conducted.
a review of a restriction order and the way in which the review is to be conducted
The following are repealed—
the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act 1966 No 31,
the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods (Poisons List) Proclamation 2016,
the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Regulation 2008.

heading.b: Members and procedures of Advisory Committees

block.txt: sections 127 and 128
In this Schedule—
Advisory Committee means—
the Clinical Advisory Committee, or
the Regulatory Advisory Committee.
A member of an Advisory Committee holds office for 3 years and is eligible, if otherwise qualified, for re-appointment.
A member of an Advisory Committee is entitled to be paid remuneration, including travelling and subsistence allowances, as determined by the Health Secretary from time to time.
The Health Secretary may, from time to time, appoint a person to act in the office of a member of an Advisory Committee during the illness or absence of the member or vacancy in the office.
While acting in the place of the member, the acting member has all the functions of the member and is taken to be a member.
The Health Secretary may remove a person from the office to which the person was appointed under this section.
The office of a member of an Advisory Committee becomes vacant if the member—
dies, or
completes a term of office and is not re-appointed, or
resigns the office by written notice to the Health Secretary, or
is removed from office by written order of the Health Secretary, or

is absent from 4 consecutive meetings of the Committee of which reasonable notice has been given to the member personally or by post, except on leave granted by the Health Secretary or unless the member is excused by the Health Secretary for having been absent from the meetings, or

becomes bankrupt, applies to take the benefit of a law for the relief of bankrupt or insolvent debtors, compounds with creditors or makes an assignment of the member’s remuneration for the creditors’ benefit, or
becomes a mentally incapacitated person, or
is convicted in New South Wales of an offence that is punishable by imprisonment for 12 months or more, or
is convicted outside of New South Wales of an offence that, if committed in New South Wales, would be punishable by imprisonment for 12 months or more.
If the office of a member of an Advisory Committee becomes vacant, a person must, subject to this Act, be appointed to fill the vacancy.
The Chairperson of an Advisory Committee must preside at a meeting of Committee.
If the Chairperson is absent from a meeting of the Committee, another member elected to chair the meeting must preside at the meeting.
The presiding member has a deliberative vote and, if there is an equality of votes, has a second or casting vote.
The Chairperson vacates office as Chairperson if the person—
resigns the office by written instrument to the Health Secretary, or
is removed from the office by the Health Secretary under this section, or
ceases to be a member of the Committee.
The Health Secretary may at any time remove the Chairperson from office as Chairperson.
A member of an Advisory Committee must—
act honestly and exercise a reasonable degree of care and diligence in carrying out the member’s functions, and
act for a proper purpose in carrying out the member’s functions, and
not use the office of member for personal advantage, and
not use the office of member to the detriment of the Committee, and

disclose interests, whether pecuniary or otherwise, that could conflict with the proper performance of the member’s functions and avoid exercising a function that could involve a conflict of interest.
This section applies to a member of a subcommittee of an Advisory Committee in the same way as it applies to a member of the Committee.
This section applies if—
a member of an Advisory Committee has a direct or indirect pecuniary interest in a matter being considered or about to be considered at a meeting of the Committee, and
the interest appears to raise a conflict with the proper performance of the member’s duties in relation to the consideration of the matter.
The member must, as soon as possible after the relevant facts have come to the member’s knowledge, disclose the nature of the interest at a meeting of the Committee.
It is sufficient disclosure of the nature of an interest relating to a specified company, body or person if the member has previously disclosed that the member—
is a member, or is in the employment, of the company or body, or
is a partner, or is in the employment, of the person, or
has some other specified interest relating to the company, body or person.

Particulars of a disclosure made under this section must be recorded by the Advisory Committee and made available to a person at all reasonable hours on payment of the fee determined by the Committee.
After a member has disclosed the nature of an interest in a matter, the member must not, unless the Health Secretary or the Advisory Committee otherwise determines—
be present during a deliberation of the Committee about the matter, or
take part in a decision of the Committee about the matter.
A member who has a direct or indirect pecuniary interest in a matter to which a disclosure relates must not—
be present at the time the Committee is making a determination for the purposes of subsection (5), or
take part in the making of the determination.
A contravention of this section does not invalidate a decision of the Advisory Committee.
This section applies to a member of a subcommittee of an Advisory Committee and the subcommittee in the same way as it applies to a member of the Committee and the Committee.
The procedure for the calling of meetings of an Advisory Committee and for the conduct of business at the meetings is, subject to this Act and the regulations, to be as determined by the Committee.
The quorum for a meeting of an Advisory Committee is a majority of the members at the time of the meeting.
A decision supported by a majority of the votes cast at a meeting of an Advisory Committee at which a quorum is present is the decision of the Committee.
The Health Secretary may call the first meeting of an Advisory Committee in the way the Health Secretary thinks fit.

heading.b: Transaction of business outside meetings or by telephone or other electronic means

block.txt: An Advisory Committee may, if it thinks fit, transact any of its business—
by the circulation of papers, by email or other electronic means, among all members, or
at a meeting at which all or some members participate by telephone, audio-visual link or other means, but only if a member who speaks on a matter at the meeting can be heard by the other members.

If an Advisory Committee transacts its business by the circulation of papers under subsection (1)(a), a written resolution approved in writing by a majority of the members is taken to be a decision of the Advisory Committee made at an Advisory Committee meeting.
For the purposes of a meeting held under subsection (1)(b) or the approval of a resolution under subsection (2), each member has the same voting rights as at an ordinary Advisory Committee meeting.
A resolution approved under subsection (2) is, subject to the regulations, to be recorded in the minutes of the Advisory Committee meeting.

heading.b: Application of Government Sector Employment Act 2013

block.txt: The provisions of the Government Sector Employment Act 2013 relating to the employment of Public Service employees do not apply to a member of an Advisory Committee.
This section applies if a provision under an Act—
requires a person who is the holder of a specified office to devote the whole of the person’s time to the duties of the office, or
prohibits the person from engaging in employment outside the duties of the office.
The provision does not operate to disqualify the person from—
holding that office and also the office of a member, or
accepting and keeping the remuneration payable to the person under this Act as a member.
The regulations may contain provisions of a savings or transitional nature consequent on the commencement of—
a provision of this Act, or
a provision amending this Act.
A savings or transitional provision consequent on the commencement of a provision must not be made more than 2 years after the commencement.
A savings or transitional provision made consequent on the commencement of a provision is repealed 2 years after the commencement.
A savings or transitional provision made consequent on the commencement of a provision may take effect before the commencement but not before—
for a provision of this Act—the date of assent to this Act, or
for a provision amending this Act—the date of assent to the amending Act.
A savings or transitional provision taking effect before its publication on the NSW legislation website does not—
affect the rights of a person existing before the publication in a way prejudicial to the person, or
impose liabilities on a person for anything done or omitted to be done before the publication.
In this section—
person does not include the State or an authority of the State.

heading.b: Provisions consequent on enactment of this Act

block.txt: In this Part—
commencement date means the date on which this Act commences.
existing wholesaler’s licence means—
a wholesaler’s licence under the former Act, or
a licence under the former Regulation, Part 8, Divisions 1–3 that authorises the wholesale supply of poisons, restricted substances or drugs of addiction under the former Act.
former Act means the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act 1966.
former Regulation means the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Regulation 2008.
new Act means the Medicines, Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act 2022.

heading.b: New obtain licences for existing wholesaler’s licences

block.txt: This section applies to a person who, immediately before the commencement date, held an existing wholesaler’s licence that authorised the person to wholesale supply a particular substance in the person’s capacity as one of the following—
a provider under the Opioid Treatment Program,
a corporation providing paramedical services,
a person providing ambulance transport with the consent of the Health Secretary under the Health Services Act 1997, section 67E,
a person providing ambulance transport who is exempt from the requirement to obtain the consent of the Health Secretary under the Health Services Act 1977, section 67E,
a person engaged in the administration of a vaccination program for humans.
The person is taken, on the commencement date, to hold an obtain licence under the new Act that authorises the person to obtain wholesale supply of the particular substance.
The obtain licence is subject to the same conditions, if any, of the existing wholesaler’s licence, subject to the regulations.
The obtain licence remains in force—
for the period specified in the existing wholesaler’s licence, if any, or
until suspended or cancelled by the Health Secretary under the new Act, Part 3.2, Division 2.

heading.b: New wholesaler licences for existing wholesaler’s licences

block.txt: This section applies to a person—
who, immediately before the commencement date, held an existing wholesaler’s licence that authorised the person to wholesale supply a particular substance, and
to whom this Schedule, section 3 does not apply.
The person is taken, on the commencement date, to hold a wholesaler licence under the new Act that authorises the person to wholesale supply the particular substance.
The wholesaler licence is subject to the same conditions, if any, of the existing wholesaler’s licence, subject to the regulations.
The wholesaler licence remains in force—
for the period specified in the existing wholesaler’s licence, if any, or
until suspended or cancelled by the Health Secretary under the new Act, Part 3.2, Division 2.
This section applies to a person who, immediately before the commencement date, was subject to an order under the former Act, section 18AA or the former Regulation, clause 175 (a former order).
The person is taken, on the commencement date, to be subject to a restriction order under the new Act, section 49.
The restriction order is taken to—
be in the same terms as the former order, and
be subject to the same conditions, if any, of the former order, and
have effect until revoked by the Health Secretary under the new Act.
To avoid doubt, the new Act, Part 2.8, other than sections 50 and 52(1), applies in relation to the restriction order.

heading.b: Exemptions for automatic machines that supply certain therapeutic goods
